A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PARCO. Their complete main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison despite the changed format and added supplementary material.

before.justification: Tables 1–2 and Figure 3 report original routing and scheduling experiments, generalization results, and component analyses.

after.justification: The original experiments are retained, with additional PARCO results on mTSP, training convergence, and larger OMDCPDP instances in Tables 4–7.

M1.justification: Sections 4.3–4.7 and Algorithm 1 retain the encoder, communication layers, multiple-pointer decoder, priority-based conflict handling, and REINFORCE training. The legacy implementation discussed in Appendix C.2 concerns newly included experiments; it does not establish a revision to the proposed algorithm.

E1.justification: Alongside the retained HCVRP, OMDCPDP, and FFSP evaluations, v3 adds min-max mTSP experiments and four mTSPLib instances. Appendix C.4 extends OMDCPDP evaluation from at most 1,000 nodes and 200 agents to 5,000 nodes and 500–1,000 agents.

E2.justification: Tables 4–5 add reported comparisons against GNN-DisPN, DAN, ScheduleNet/SchedNet, LKH3, CPLEX, and HGA, which were not evaluated against PARCO in v2. Comparator membership in the retained Tables 1–2 is unchanged.

E3.justification: Existing Appendix B settings remain unchanged. New XXL tests use 16 instances per agent count, a one-hour OR-Tools budget, and greedy neural decoding; convergence is evaluated at five training-budget fractions. Figure 3b changes the reported timing measure from training minutes to seconds per epoch, without establishing that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix C.3 adds validation-cost convergence analysis across all three original problems. Appendix C.4 adds generalization tests at 50 times the training scale. These substantially extend the retained component ablations and earlier 10-times-scale generalization analysis.

E5.justification: Figure 3 already has error bars in v2, but v3's checklist newly identifies them as standard deviations from three seeds; this does not establish increased run counts. Table 6 also introduces numerical ± reporting without defining its meaning or associated run count.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 are unchanged, while Tables 4–7 add mTSP scores, convergence measurements, and XXL results. For example, Table 5 reports average gaps of 5.22% for PARCO and 8.55% for SchedNet; Table 7 reports PARCO's objective of 1726.78 in 0.22 seconds at 5,000 nodes and 1,000 agents. These are additional results, not same-setting improvements over v2.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.3 and Equation (2) explicitly formulate expected-reward optimization and define the instance distribution P(x). v3 removes this formal statement, retaining a brief verbal objective in Section 3.2. The remaining method equations and Appendix A formulations remain mathematically equivalent.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: a general parallel autoregressive framework, its three principal components, and improved solution quality and efficiency for multi-agent routing and scheduling. Revised wording and additional supporting experiments do not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: Appendix C.2 newly qualifies the mTSP results as using an older, faulty conflict handler and acknowledges that ET and DPN would outperform that implementation. It adds interpretations about centralized coordination and GNN overhead, while C.3–C.4 discuss training stability and extreme-scale applicability. The original limitation requiring a specified agent count remains.

D1.justification: The detailed hyperparameters, hardware, software, and source-code access information in Appendix B are retained. v3 additionally discloses the legacy implementation issue, provides mTSPLib access information, and reports checkpoint release through HuggingFace in its checklist.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands research positioning through cooperative Markov-game references in Section 4.1, discussion of PARCO follow-ups such as CAMP, USPR, and MACSIM, and connections to LLM-designed heuristics and search methods in Appendix C.1. These additions extend beyond bibliographic updates to existing citations.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section order are retained. v3 revises the title, affiliations, abstract, and selected analysis passages; condenses the RL preliminaries; renames Section 4.1; and adds Appendix C and a checklist. Much of the additional text documents new scientific content rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from two-column to single-column layout. Figure 1 is simplified and relocated, Figure 3 is redrawn, and Figure 4 gains speedup annotations and revised styling. v3 adds the Seoul map and Tables 4–7; the existing FFSP decoding diagram is retained as Figure 6.

improvement.justification: The additional benchmarks, convergence analysis, extreme-scale tests, and Figure 3 uncertainty disclosure strengthen v2's evidence and transparency. Gains are limited by the legacy mTSP implementation, undefined Table 6 uncertainties, and an inconsistent Table 7 OR-Tools gap at 750 agents: 115.24% is listed, while its objective values imply approximately 171.11%. The core method and main result tables remain unchanged.
